newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Zeitler warns against EMU window-dressing.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Zeitler warns against EMU window-dressing.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler added his voice on Monday to the chorus of German policy makers warning nations against window-dressing finances to join Europe's currency union.
Zeitler, stressing that time pressure to join the union in the next decade should be turned into pressure to improve quality, said so-called creative accounting would not be helpful for the union.

"The new currency needs trust and its base capital must be the credibility that stability will be maintained, creative accounting and a loose interpretation of the criteria can only weaken the currency's acceptance among European citizens and markets," Zeitler said.

According to the Maastricht Treaty, nations intending to join the single currency in 1999 must aim for a government deficit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and a government debt to GDP ratio of 60 percent, based on 1997 data.
Zeitler, also the president of the state central bank in Bavaria, made his comments in an article to be published in the next edition of the magazine "Politische Studien."

Germany has been a vocal opponent of nations' last minute efforts to whip their finances into shape and pass the strict entry criteria to be among the first nations to enter the currency union in 1999.

At the same time, Zeitler warned the concept of shareholder value, which has been eagerly adopted by many German managers, could be counter-productive if it is misused by managers focusing only on short-term returns.
Zeitler warned that research and worker training must not be reduced in favour of improving shareholder value.

The concept of raising shareholder value has swept the German industry with managers at large corporations ranging from Daimler-Benz AG to Hoechst AG all saying they plan to do everything possible to increase shareholder value.
On the other hand, Zeitler said Germany needs a properly functioning labour market with a wage structure that is flexible and able to react to the needs of the company.
The European currency union will not offer a short-term improvement in the labour market. But the common currency is a key component for long-term growth, he added.
